videos.title: jamie fernandez   effective warm ups for youth performance players (1080p)

segments.description: Coaches, it's my pleasure to introduce Dr. Jaime Fernandez, a highly respected expert in exercise and sports sciences with over 15 years of experience in athlete development. Dr. Fernandez holds a PhD in exercise and sports sciences and serves as a senior lecturer at the University of Leon, Spain. He has worked as a strength and conditioning specialist with elite athletes including ATP and WTA top 100 players and is head of strength and conditioning at the International Abadminton Technification Centre in Oviedo, Spain. Today he will share his insights on effective warm-ups for youth performance players, a vital aspect of preparing young athletes for success. Welcome Jaime. My name is Jaime Fernandez Fernandez and I'm going to talk about neuromuscular training in youth tennis players. First of all I would like to thank Tennis Australia for inviting me to this nice virtual tennis conference and I hope you enjoy the presentation. First of all of course I would like to present who am I. As I told you my name is Jaime Fernandez. I've been working as a lecturer at different universities for many years. I'm actually working at the University of Leon as a senior lecturer at the Faculty of Sports Science and I've been also working and collaborating with different tennis federations in terms of scientific consultancy. In the practical field I've been working with athletes for many many years almost more

than 20 years already as not only as a consultant for different athletes, teams or federations but also directly on court with different types of tennis players from juniors or even younger to professional tennis players. So basically my goal was always to try to find these or feel this gap between science and practical experience or try to bring scientific information into the field which is not an easy question. As you can see here I mean sometimes you have to face different questions and basically for me the most important things are to face what do you want to do with the athlete versus what do you really need to do with the athlete. Sometimes you have a lot of information coming from science but it's not possible to do like research or to do some practical applications with your athletes because your athletes actually need some other things. Also what could you do because we can actually do many many things based on research versus what you should do with your athletes with the time you have which sometimes is really short with the materials you have or even with the schedules. So it's not easy to find this nice picture of what would you like to do and sometimes I feel like what I want is utopia but this is what I'm basically trying to do and it's not easy because you have to face the theoretical background you can find with the evidence face approach which is sometimes difficult for the coaches, difficult for the strength

of the coaching coaches to understand what is written in those articles and it's very difficult to put it into practice. So as I said you have to face theory versus practice because the reality at the end of the day as you can see here in this video is that we work with many many athletes sometimes course different sexes and different ages all at the same time with not so many stuff or material sometimes before practice or specific practice or sometimes after specific practice. So it is nice to write papers and to put to put out some scientific knowledge that the question we must do is okay why we do that and we do that because of ourselves or because of others and we want to progress at the university or we want to put some practical information into the sports science field and put out some information which can reach actually the coaches and the athletes so this is something really interesting to put it out. So then again coming from science we have this evidence based approach which means that you know you take the data resulting from different studies and control trials that you see here expert or user consensus evaluation anecdotal information and you try to put that into the real training environments but I feel like it's more useful at least for me and this what they call practice based approach which is okay you take some information from coming from science but you also ask the coach and you ask the athlete and you take that into account

their opinions their expertise their characteristics their values and context and you try to put that into the training program so I would say that I'm trying to do this practice based approach so once we have that information more or less clear what we have to do is to analyze deeply the demands of our sport in this case tennis basically this is the more or less the the schedule or the follow-up we need or I use to follow up when I design or construct training programs first is to analyze the physical workload of competition and training so we have to know basically about the demands of the sport and in our case no matter if the athlete is a professional or is a young athlete what we have in tennis is intermittent sport which combines a lot of different things strength power speed agility we also need like a good aerobic aerobic based plus a lot of different capacities including flexibility and coordination all mixed in the same package so to be successful these athletes need to accelerate decelerate change direction and repeatedly produce power in terms of stroke for many many hours the second step of this diagram is to know once we know about the physical demands of the sport to know which kind of characteristics are needed in terms of physical performance or which are the most important characteristics for for athletes in our case we basically we basically work with kids that means that we are working with pre around and post pure players specific with adolescence

players then we have to think about this because we have all these players mixed up in the training and it's not the best scenario possible then we have to think about if tennis is an early specialization sport which for me is not I mean of course we need like an early initiation like I say here but definitely like some other sports is a late specialization sport so we have time enough and since you can see here if you analyze the top 50 the ATP and WTA level the ages are pretty okay not so young we're talking about 26 28 years old so we have from these adolescence ages till they can reach the top levels we're talking about a lot of time to invest in develop so definitely a tennis is not an early specialization sport and we know based on science that early specialization leads to a lot of problems including the increase of injury risk including the early burnout syndrome including an impaired overall athletic performance even if we have really you know really talented players who are like really good early ages but then we have to think about the future the future means that in a couple of years they will be probably show like impaired performance compared to the peers so definitely tennis is not an early specialization sport and we cannot look for that then second question here is to analyze where are we I mean as I told you we are at the stages of you know puberty so it's important to detect and try to

calculate where we are so here in this picture there's a nice example of that these are two German players same age actually the player on the left is older and the player on the right but as you can see the player on the right is an early material compared to the player on the left who is a late material so that actually they have like around six or seven years difference but they have the same chronological age so that's important in terms of training for these players so the next step is to establish a fitness training priorities in these ages so we have like a lot of information coming from science and really nice models to follow in terms of training and I highly recommend this one the youth physical development model wrote by Joyd and Oliver and there is a nice book about this strength and conditioning for young athletes which is a good reference for for us as a strength and conditioning coaches this manual we can see which are the most interesting fitness qualities to develop depending on the ages and depending on the peak high velocity maturation point so what we should work when they are at the pre around or post peak high velocity so in terms of correlations with performance there are like several studies analyzing what is important at different ages as you can see here even if the graphics are a little bit complex there are like repeated fitness qualities over and over again no matter if the girls or boys are younger or a little bit

older and it's the sprint jumping capacities so neuromuscular capacities so in terms of speed and change of direction and jumping power there was a recent research analyzing a lot of junior tennis players you see here almost 1500 young tennis players boys and girls which found that the change of direction speed was the most impactful factor for tennis performance so the correlation between change of direction speed and the ranking was really high meaning that this is a very important quality to develop this stage so at the same time the change of direction speed was strongly influenced by the linear spin and jumping power so it means that these neuromuscular qualities are very important at young ages so remember first to analyze the demands of the sport then to analyze okay what is important for our players including the maturation status including which qualities are more important and analyzing that we see that change of direction is a really important quality you can see here are two videos of boy and a girl at same age a little bit differences in terms of biological maturation but they have the same chronological age as you can see there are many many differences in terms of change of direction not only about performance but also also about technique and if we analyze one by one and technique is so important in terms of running so I made a picture and you can see in the change of direction technique at

these ages it's fundamental so we need to invest a lot of time working on the basics we made a study a couple of years ago about you know simple change of direction this is the 505 tests 180 degrees change of direction and as you can see here in the results we compare only chronological ages under 13 and under 15 boys and girls and as you can see there are like differences in terms of performance especially at the ages of under 15 but in terms of change of direction when the players are younger there are not too many differences and these differences in the change of direction performance in this case the deficit which is the difference between the linear spring and the change of direction so we normally compare 10 meter spring linear and then we do like 55 this is the 505 test 5 and then 5 back so if you analyze here there are no differences between boys and girls at the age of 12 but at the age of 14 these differences are significantly increased so the females are slower in the change of direction compared to male so this is something to take into account because normally we train players organized by age chronological age and and also we mix that boys and girls and what we can take into account is that there are not only biological differences at these ages but also performance differences mostly caused by these biological differences so in an attempt to to increase the knowledge of these differences in terms of change of direction there

are not only differences between boys and girls but also differences between groups at different stages of maturation like I said we have three groups like pre peak high velocity around peak high velocity and post peak high velocity so what we can see here is that players who are like biologically younger let's say that their physical qualities are poorer poorer compared to the other groups and post peak high velocity so if we organize our players only by chronological age we're gonna have a lot of problems and most of these problems are caused because you know the the maturation groups are not the same and even if we put the same players or different players in the same court we have to take that into account once we do that we can analyze a lot of differences so in terms of different things of direction a test this is the pro agility test can consider it a little bit more specific in terms of tennis that's so specific but there are a few more changes of direction and what we can see is that it's not only about the differences between maturation or groups it's also about the amount of deficit in the change of direction these players accumulate when they do the second change of direction so this one would be the first change of direction a player will come here and perform the second change of direction so sometimes in some cases some players especially the younger ones biologically

they accumulate more than 100 percent of deficit so that means that they are like 100 percent slow we're going to perform this part of the test this one compared to the first change of direction so this is another practical application we can get from from that so first is remember to analyze where we are and what we need so based on this information okay how we can improve that you know we're talking about linear spring speed we are talking about a change of direction we are jumping power we're talking about specificity in terms of gender or sex so well i mean there's the neuromuscular training neuromuscular training is the combination of different you know fitness qualities including speed agility stability we can also include here flexibility strength plyometrics related to strength that's four specific exercises and of course i'm all the qualities like cognitive ability so we put all these together and we call it neuromuscular training and we know that is a very efficient way of working with especially a young athlete and so which is the first way to work with these athletes in terms of strength i would say that plyometrics is the first one we have these you know scientific or sound based information of what to do at the different ages of maturation and what we know is that the inclusion of you know plyometric training since early ages is a very important you know tool for developing good athletes in terms of tennis we've been working quite a lot

with this kind of workouts in this case what you see here is the is a study we conducted with our pre peak high velocity players which were around who were around sorry 12.5 years old 60 tennis players they were they were training two times per week for eight weeks and this is the training program including basically jumps easy jumps and some upper body exercises which were basically medicine ball throws we started doing like 30 minute workout and finishing the last couple of weeks doing 40 to 45 minute workout which is quite a long but it's quite a long workout but i mean at the time we thought it was the the best way to develop these qualities what we found is that you know organizing a little bit these these workouts only for eight weeks all the players improved quite a lot in their physical qualities and you can see here the percentage of changes in all the tests conducted and for example in the surf velocity test they increased 6 to 6.2 percent after the training program so we found that this is a very very interesting way of working with with players but like i said before i mean 45 minutes maybe it's too much we normally don't have so much time to work with these these players especially only one quality so what we are trying to do now is based on other research and other recommendations and other sports trying to find these you know these micro dosing what is a micro dosing

it's basically what you can read here is it's basically the minimum dose that develops or at least maintains the capacity we want to develop or maintain in athletes no matter if you're a young athlete or a professional in terms of young athletes of course we would need like to find this what is the minimal dose to develop some some qualities but this is what is micro dosing okay we've been working on that also for many years in tennis and we found that a combination simple combination of plyometrics and repeated sprints in this case overall workout which took more or less 30 to 35 minutes and conducted two or three times a week in the in-season period led to really good results in in terms of performance for a junior player these these are where post-peach high-velocity tennis players so as you can see here they improved the acceleration part of 10 meter sprint they improved the counter movement jump and they improved repeated sprint ability so yeah more or less 30 to 35 minutes of these kind of workouts seems to be very very effective then it comes another question of course we know that this kind of workouts are efficient and are important for these young tennis players but what was an important question for me a long time ago was okay sometimes we have like I said at the beginning of the presentation sometimes we have players who are coming to you at the you know before tennis and

some of the players they come to you after tennis for fitness so I was always thinking that maybe this is not the best way you know depending on which are the contains the training contents you have for that day if you have players who are coming after tennis your your training probably will be compromised so what we did was to to analyze the effects of the intra-season sequence so basically for five weeks we have one group who was doing tennis and then they were doing this kind of neuromuscular training and another group was doing neuromuscular training and then tennis what happened as you can expect is that those players who were doing fitness before tennis were the only ones who were improving compared to those players who were doing fitness or this kind of neuromuscular training after tennis so those who were doing this training after tennis some of them they even got worse so that's that's an important result to take into account so always if you want to develop neuromuscular training you know qualities players should train if possible before tennis okay so some of the questions if we need 30 minutes or 35 minutes stops and we know that neuromuscular trainings should be developed before tennis why not to take advantage of the warm-up I mean the warm-up is the basics for everything and it's for me it's the the first preventive weapon we have so why not to include all these exercises in the in the

warm-up program and and do it like repeatedly for for a few weeks and let's see what happened so we took some tennis players and you see here the the characteristics 28 boys average age of 15 years old more or less and we conducted this neuromuscular warm-up program for eight weeks and they've been doing it for four days a week so we compared two groups the neuromuscular training program combined you know activation general and thoracic mobility core hip and shoulder strength and then upper lower body plyometrics acceleration deceleration change of direction drills for five to eight minutes which you know block compared to classical dynamic warm-up they do mobility ballistic exercises some shoulder strength and then they go into the court and do the specific let's say a warm-up what we found is that both warm-ups were like interesting to improve for example spring and counter movement jump medicine ball throw and some some shoulder strength values and range of motion values in the shoulder but comparing both the neuromuscular warm-up program produced a greater performance gains in most of the analyzed parameters especially the acceleration part of the sprint counter movement jump medicine ball throw or serve a speed so we can say and conclude that these kind of warm-up approaches are very efficient for these players we want a little bit more deeper into this warm-up approach and a few years ago we conducted a study also with young players

including not only the warm-up as let's say a part to improve performance in players but also to include some injury prevention approach so what we did as you can see here we included not only the general mobility part then the strength core strength hip strength shoulder strength but also we include some exercises using some you know technology inertial technology using these aversa pulley and eccentric overload devices and what we saw is that we can also use the warm-up as a injury prevention weapon you can see here players who conducted this is the the versa pulley the devices I told you about and some of the exercises we conducted players who were conducting these warm-up programs they improved the internal external rotation parameters and the dominant shoulder like you know almost an external rotation dominant side more than 20% increases in strength levels and they reduced the external rotation internal rotation ratio which is a you know injury risk parameter and they also improved quite a lot the shoulder range of motion because at the end of the of the training they individualized stretching program so we can also use the warm-up as a you know injury prevention weapon then some other questions came to our mind in terms of you know practical approach and this neuromuscular training approach is okay normally I don't know in Australia but in Spain normally players and young players they do tennis training and at the end of the training

tennis training session they they do surf training they basically do all the volume for the surf training at the end of the session okay this is changing somehow in the last few years but there are still many many places many clubs many players are still doing that so that was another question for research so what we basically did was to analyze a pre-post intervention what will happen between two groups first group was doing the the warm-up specific warm-up shoulder warm-up and then they were doing the surf training and then tennis training on the other side there was another group doing the warm-up doing tennis training and doing the typical surf training at the end of the session what we measure was a surf speed accuracy shoulder strength and shoulder range of range of motion and then we they've been doing this for for a few weeks and what we found is you know that for those players who were doing the surf training after tennis there were there was a reduction in all the important parameters not only related to performance but also to injury or injury prevention drastically compared to those players who were you know training surf before the specific tennis session like I said we analyze shoulder strength and shoulder range of motion you can see here there are like significant decreases in all the parameters so as a practical recommendation if you can do that please do the warm-up the specific like shoulder

warm-up surf warm-up and then train before tennis session or in the middle of the tennis session but never at the end if possible so I'm going to find you know interesting to present these latest results we've been publishing the last few years because you know in terms of the practical approach of fitness training in tennis there was always like confusion between different training programs and and one of the things I always tell to coaches is that many many ways lead to wrong right so we basically we've been comparing different training programs using let's say typical exercises you can see in fitness coaches the first one was to compare the effects of resistance versus conventional sprint training in elite tennis young tennis players so that's typical one of the typical exercises we do we all do with tennis players using the elastics or using some weighted vests or elastic cords so we basically compared training program similar training program using this weighted vests or using elastic cords versus no material so just doing the sprints with no equipment and no resistance and what we basically found was that there were not too many differences between programs so yeah okay in terms of resisted versus conventional sprint training we can see that there were like some extra benefits using these elastics and weighted vests in terms of acceleration in terms of some jumps but overall there are not too many differences so like I said many ways lead to wrong we can select

different training approaches based on what we want or what we need for those players uh another typical training approach used in tennis is the use of sand I mean we see that many players even really young players they they train in soft surfaces like like sand so what we did was to compare exactly the same same training program you can see here combining plyometrics some running technique or abc and acceleration, deceleration, change of direction drills for a six-week period one group was doing that on sand and the other group was doing it on a regular hard surface again like the resisted sprint versus conventional sprint we found that both training strategies were similar in terms of improvement of course there were some slight differences between surfaces so for example the harshest phases favored you know changes or produced significantly higher changes in counter movement jumps and repeated jumps and reactive strength index so if we want to improve that we should think about use using hard surfaces but in terms of sand training or sand training improve the more dynamic balance of the players as well as the adductor and adductor hip strength so basically again like I said at the beginning this is uh you know to put in front two questions okay what we want to obtain or versus what we need to obtain also to take into account that training in sand if especially if the players

are not used to because higher training load and muscle soreness compared to hard surface this is basically because players were not used to so to to finish my presentation some take home messages first of course is to use the maturity states the calculation of the peak high velocity instead of chronological age it could be more appropriate when when designing our training programs basically that foundational strength and movement skills are essential for for development players strength training is the first you know approach to to develop players and leads to increases in limb body mass which is also interesting in order to improve these athleticism of our players your muscular players for example training sorry for example these resist the springs originally directed power exercises eccentric strength training change of direction training is a very efficient way of working with youth athletes and I would say that exercises focus on the specific movement movement technique to improve efficiency during these uh change of direction in different angles of direction is highly recommended and the change of direction workouts could include all these parameters to to to be more efficient combining cognitive physical and technical aspects of of the movement so thank you very much for your attention I hope you enjoyed the presentation for any question you have here my information I really
appreciate your attention and muchas gracias
